statedGuarantee: MiniScope sits between a tool-calling LLM agent and the user's connected SaaS services as a mediation point that holds the user's real OAuth credentials and hands the agent only a session token. It reconstructs a permission hierarchy from each service's published OAuth scope documentation, solves an integer linear program to compute the minimal set of scopes required by the agent's submitted execution plan, prompts the user (mobile-style: Always allow / Allow once / Allow this session / Don't allow) for any scope not already granted, and then intercepts every tool call, forwarding it with the real credential only if it falls inside the granted permission state. The formal guarantee, stated as a security game in which the adversary picks the LLM and injects malicious data into service state, is: 'we say the system is secure if, for every step j , all tool calls in c_{j} are permitted under \rho_{j} .' The paper explicitly disclaims defending against prompt injection generally, against attacks that stay inside an already-granted scope, and against multi-agent settings.
advertisedRhetoric: our enforcement is mechanical and provides rigorous guarantees
tierSpan: We wrap each MCP function with a decorator that validates whether the tool call is permitted under the currently granted permissions.
cheapestDefeat: Tier work-through. GUARANTEE: every tool call the agent actually executes on a service is authorized by the permission state the user granted. MECHANISM THAT MUST FAIL: the Permission Checker, implemented as a decorator wrapping each MCP function, plus the credential-substitution step that swaps the agent's session token for the user's real bearer token ('Before a tool call reaches the service, it is intercepted by the Permission Checker, which verifies the request using the granted permissions associated with the session token stored in the Credential Storage.'). CHEAPEST ADVERSARY ACTION: not forging anything. Two defeats, both cheap, neither requiring the checker to be broken. (a) Stay inside an already-granted scope: the checker's predicate is scope membership, not intent, so an injected plan that reuses a scope the user already approved (e.g. a gmail send scope granted for a legitimate summarizing task, then reused to exfiltrate) passes every check. The paper concedes exactly this: 'MiniScope does not provide guarantees against attacks that alter the execution plan within the currently granted permissions.' (b) Reach the effector by a path that never traverses the decorator: the agent is an ordinary LangGraph process with a command line and network access, unconfined by any OS mechanism; nothing in the design stops it or any descendant from writing local files, spawning processes, or making direct network requests to a service not registered with MiniScope. MECHANISM DEFEATED BY THE CHEAPEST ACTION: an application-level chokepoint in the tool-call path. Therefore T3. Note the charitable T1 reading that is available and that I nonetheless rejected: the paper argues token unforgeability ('under the security assumption of the authentication protocol, the probability of an agent correctly guessing a valid credential is negligible') and isolates real bearer tokens from the agent, which is a genuine cryptographic property. But the weakest-link rule governs: forging the session token is unnecessary when a compliant, honestly issued token authorizes the harmful call, and when unmediated paths exist entirely outside the token system. This matches the rubric's worked example, where a signed capability enforced by an in-process hook scores T3.
placementSpan: In MiniScope, we do not trust the underlying LLM used by the agent, nor the responses from connected services, since the model may hallucinate or be subject to prompt injection, and service responses may contain attacker controlled data.

coverageSpans.E1: MiniScope targets 10 real, widely-used applications: Gmail, Google Calendar, Google Drive, Google Storage, Slack, Dropbox, Outlook, Outlook Calendar, Notion, and Zoom.
coverageSpans.E3: Requested tool calls are forwarded to the target service using the user’s real credentials only if they are permitted under the granted permissions.
coverageSpans.E6: User credentials for accessing services are fully isolated from the agent to prevent direct exploitation by attacker.
coverageSpans.E7: In this paper, we focus on single agent systems, leaving multi-agent scenarios, where multiple agents communicate on behalf of their users, to future work.

coverageReasoning.E1: partial. Remote file mutation on a registered service (Google Drive, Google Storage, Dropbox, Notion) is genuinely mediated: a write method maps to an OAuth scope and the decorator rejects it if that scope is not granted. That is real coverage for those instances. But local filesystem writes by the agent process or any descendant are never named and never reached; nothing in the design constrains the host. Reaches some instances and provably not others, so partial, not covered. The covert-channel rule caps it independently: within a granted write scope, an injected plan can overwrite or delete anything that scope permits, which the paper concedes is out of scope.
coverageReasoning.E2: not-covered. Subprocess spawn is nowhere in the paper. There is no process boundary, no seccomp, no namespace, no exec mediation of any kind; the effector is simply not addressed. Per the rubric this scores not-covered rather than not-applicable.
coverageReasoning.E3: partial. Egress to a registered service is chokepointed and credential-bound, so the agent cannot reach Gmail or Slack with the user's real token outside the granted scopes, which is meaningful control over the credentialed channel. It provably does not reach: (i) arbitrary egress from the agent process or any descendant to any host not registered with MiniScope, and (ii) exfiltration through a granted scope, e.g. sending mail under an approved send scope. Point (ii) is exactly the covert-channel rule: the stated contract excludes the channel, honestly and explicitly ('It does not directly prevent attacks that attempt to mislead the model into issuing additional tool calls that remain within the same scope.'), and honesty does not close the gap. Ceiling is partial.
coverageReasoning.E4: not-covered. No version-control service is among the ten applications and git push is never discussed. Not addressed.
coverageReasoning.E5: not-covered. Package install, third-party install hooks, and their network activity are never discussed. Not addressed.
coverageReasoning.E6: partial. This is MiniScope's strongest cell and the one I most nearly scored covered. The design does hold the real OAuth credentials out of the agent entirely, hands it only a session token, and substitutes the credential at the mediation point: 'This design ensures that the agent never directly accesses the user’s actual bearer tokens.' The credential list is effectively published, being the enumerated set of services registered in Credential Storage with hierarchies derived from public OAuth documentation. But the depth rule asks for coverage over the credential surface, and the host's environment variables, config files, keychain, and any cloud metadata endpoint are channels the system does not name and does not reach; an agent process steered by injection can read them without touching MiniScope. Reaches some instances and provably not others: partial.
coverageReasoning.E7: not-covered. Explicitly deferred to future work. The design assumes a single agent registering one session with MiniScope, and there is no mechanism by which a spawned sub-agent would inherit, be constrained by, or be visible to the permission state.

schneider.surrogate: A per-call safety property checkable by a reference monitor: at every step, each executed tool call must be a member of the currently granted scope set. Stated formally in the security game as 'we say the system is secure if, for every step j , all tool calls in c_{j} are permitted under \rho_{j}', and implemented as the Permission Checker decorator plus credential substitution. This sits squarely inside Schneider's EM-enforceable class: a prefix-closed predicate on the execution trace, decidable at each step from the current state.
schneider.objective: The advertised objective is damage confinement under an untrusted model and untrusted data: 'MiniScope aims to confine potential harm caused by the tool-calling agent to the user’s connected services' and, in the abstract, 'confining potential damage from unreliable LLMs.' Whether an action constitutes harm depends on the user's intent and on where the user's data ends up, which is an information-flow hyperproperty, not a property of any single trace, and therefore not monitor-enforceable. The paper is unusually honest about the gap rather than papering over it: 'MiniScope provides security guarantees only at the granularity defined by the permission hierarchy', and it does not prevent misuse of an already-granted scope. Split, with both halves named by the authors themselves.

notes:
CORPUS-RELEVANT FINDING (the reason this paper is in the T-12 SoK): the mobile-permission analogy is load-bearing rhetoric here and it imports OS-grade binding expectations the mechanism does not deliver. The paper says 'we draw inspiration from the permission model used by modern mobile operating systems' and 'we adopt the permission model used in modern mobile platforms.' On Android or iOS, a denied permission is enforced by the kernel against the process regardless of the app's intent, a T2 bound. Here the borrowed object is only the CONSENT UX (Always allow / Allow once / Allow this session / Don't allow) plus the coarse grouping semantics; the enforcement substrate underneath is an in-process decorator wrapping MCP functions plus a credential-substituting relay. A user who has internalized 'this is like app permissions on my phone' will over-read the binding. Being fair to the authors: they never claim OS or kernel enforcement, and the analogy is drawn explicitly and only to the permission MODEL, not to the enforcement mechanism. The over-reading is imported by the reader, not asserted by the text. That is a cleaner failure mode than most of the corpus and should be recorded as such.

WHERE I WAS UNCERTAIN, in order of how much it could move the coding:
1. advertisedTier. I scored T3, i.e. the paper advertises what it delivers, which is unusually well calibrated. Two things pulled toward a higher advertised tier and I rejected both: (a) the mobile-OS analogy connotes T2, but per the paragraph above the text does not claim it; (b) the formal security game with negligible-probability token-guessing arguments connotes T1, but the game's own definition of secure is a scope-membership predicate, which is a T3-shaped claim dressed in cryptographic notation. An adjudicator who counts connotation as advertisement would score advertisedTier T2 and open a real advertised-versus-scored gap. I did not, under the charitable stance.
2. E6. Strong case for 'covered' within the paper's own declared system boundary, since the credential list IS enumerated and the isolation is genuine. I held at partial only because the effector definition explicitly includes env, config, keychain, and metadata endpoint, none of which MiniScope reaches. If the corpus intends E6 to mean 'credentials for the services the system mediates', this cell should be covered.
3. evidenceGrade L2 versus L1. There is no adversarial evaluation anywhere in this paper. The three evaluation axes are permission minimality against an LLM baseline, latency overhead (1-6 percent), and simulated user confirmation rate; the single attack in the paper is an illustrative figure ('Fig. 5: Example of an in-scope attack that MiniScope defends against'), not a run. I graded L2 charitably because the system is implemented end to end in roughly 8,000 lines of Python, the enforcement path is exercised in every measured run, and the solver empirically found six overprivileged real-world connector deployments in shipping ChatGPT and Claude connectors, which is behavioral confirmation that the mechanism functions. But the SECURITY claim specifically is at L1: argued from design, never tested against an attacker. A stricter coder should record L1 and would be defensible.
4. adversaryPlacementPrimary A2. Chosen because the design's security analysis and its worked example both center untrusted data arriving through the prompt or through tool responses. A3 is formally modeled (the security game lets the adversary choose f_LLM outright, a stronger placement claim than most papers make) but is not tested either, so it sits as secondary. A1 is secondary as the ambient case. No placement is actually adversarially evaluated, so 'the one the evaluation actually tests' is arguably empty; A2 is the one the design argues about.

OTHER THINGS AN ADJUDICATOR SHOULD KNOW:
- Scope of applicability. This is a SaaS-connector authorization layer (Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Google Storage, Slack, Dropbox, Outlook, Outlook Calendar, Notion, Zoom, over MCP), not a coding-harness confinement layer. Five of the seven ACTION-SURFACE effectors are outside its problem statement entirely. The coding above is not a criticism of the paper for failing at something it never attempted; it is a map of what the guarantee reaches.
- The service-correctness assumption is a real dependency: 'MiniScope assumes that their tool call implementations follow the intended specifications.' A service whose method does more than its documented scope implies silently widens every bound. The authors bound the blast radius honestly: a bad service cannot compromise other services on the same agent.
- The permission hierarchy is derived from vendor OAuth documentation scraped from public websites, not from a verified contract. Granularity is therefore hostage to how coarsely a vendor drew its scopes. The authors name this and propose method-level and argument-level (action by target) refinement as future work in VII-B.
- Reproducibility of retrieval: full text obtained from the arXiv LaTeXML HTML render of v1 (arXiv:2512.11147v1 [cs.CR], 11 Dec 2025, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0), converted to text locally. Every span in this file was byte-verified against that extraction before being recorded. Two spans contain a Unicode right single quote (U+2019) carried over verbatim from the source rather than normalized to ASCII.
